bib.title: UniIR: Training and Benchmarking Universal Multimodal Information Retrievers

read.skipped: Appendix Figures 7-16 (per-dataset retrieval visualisations) and the numeric bodies of Tables 11-13 (Recall@1/5/10 per dataset) were skimmed only; the venue is not printed anywhere in the PDF (arXiv stamp 'arXiv:2311.17136v1 [cs.CV] 28 Nov 2023').

question: Can one instruction-following retriever handle queries and candidates of any modality (text, image, image+text) across diverse retrieval tasks, and how should such retrievers be trained and benchmarked?
hypothesis: Multi-task training plus natural-language task instructions lets a single retriever pick the intended modality and task from a heterogeneous pool and generalise to unseen datasets and tasks.
contributions: UniIR Framework: A universal multimodal information retrieval framework designed to integrate various multimodal retrieval tasks into a cohesive system.
M-BEIR: A large-scale multimodal retrieval benchmark that assembles 10 diverse datasets from multiple domains, encompassing 8 distinct multimodal retrieval tasks.
UniIR models: universal retrievers trained on M-BEIR as a baseline, plus zero-shot evaluation of SOTA vision-language pre-trained models on M-BEIR.

method.summary: UniIR fine-tunes CLIP ViT-L/14 and BLIP (large) dual encoders with an in-batch query-candidate contrastive loss on the M-BEIR training split, with a natural-language task instruction prefixed to the query text. Two fusion variants are used (score-level: weighted sum of per-modality similarities; feature-level: a mixed-modality fusion module that outputs one vector). Evaluation is Recall@k with FAISS retrieval from either the 5.6M global pool or per-dataset local pools.
method.task: instruction-following universal multimodal retrieval (8 task types over text, image and image-text queries/candidates)

datasets.name: M-BEIR
datasets.size: 10 datasets, 8 tasks, 4 domains, 64 instructions; train 1.1M, dev 182K, test 190K queries; global pool 5.6M candidates (text says 1.5 million queries in total)
datasets.split: original splits of each dataset; if a dataset releases only a validation set, part of train is held out for validation and results are reported on the original validation set
datasets.source: Repurposes VisualNews, MSCOCO, Fashion200K, WebQA, EDIS, NIGHTS, OVEN, InfoSeek, FashionIQ, CIRR (licences not stated)
datasets.preprocessing: Distorted text/images removed, images resized to 256 pixels on the shorter side; larger datasets (VisualNews, OVEN, InfoSeek) trimmed in instances and candidate pools; OVEN candidate text = Wikipedia title + first 100 tokens of summary; InfoSeek articles split into 100-token snippets; 4 human-authored instructions per task-dataset pair; M-BEIR (5.6M) pool = union of the ten M-BEIR_local pools

datasets.name: M-BEIR_local
datasets.size: task-specific homogeneous candidate pools from each original dataset (e.g. MSCOCO 25K text + 5K images; NIGHTS 40K images; EDIS 1M; OVEN and InfoSeek trimmed from 6M to 1M each)

datasets.name: Held-out generalisation split
datasets.size: train on 7 held-in datasets; test on 3 held-out datasets (WebQA, OVEN, CIRR) covering tasks 2, 3, 6, 7, 8
datasets.split: WebQA, OVEN, CIRR excluded from fine-tuning

models.name: UniIR CLIP_SF
models.architecture: CLIP ViT-L/14 image and text encoders, score-level fusion (weighted sum of four similarity terms)

models.name: UniIR CLIP_FF
models.architecture: CLIP encoders plus a 2-layer T5-style multimodal transformer f_MIX (12 attention heads, 64 dims per head), randomly initialised

models.name: UniIR BLIP_FF
models.architecture: BLIP ViT-L/14 image encoder feeding the cross-attention layers of BLIP's image-grounded text encoder as f_MIX

models.name: Zero-shot CLIP (L-14), SigLIP (L, timm/ViT-L-16-SigLIP-256), BLIP (L), BLIP2
models.architecture: pretrained vision-language encoders used as feature extractors, no instruction

other.task8: only the image used for query and candidate; candidate text is the Wikipedia title with prompt 'a picture of [title]'

models.name: Multi-task baselines (CLIP_SF, CLIP_FF, BLIP_SF, BLIP_FF)
models.architecture: same architectures as UniIR, trained on all M-BEIR train data without instructions

training.objective: in-batch query-candidate contrastive loss maximising positive pair similarity; instruction prefixed to the query text; padding tokens input for missing modalities

other.hyperparameters: 'other hyperparameters as reported in the original implementations' (not listed)

inference.samples: single run per configuration; no seeds or variance reported
inference.prompting: one of 4 human-written instructions per task-dataset pair prefixed to the query text; zero-shot baselines get no instruction (instructions degraded zero-shot retrieval)
inference.retrieval: two-step pipeline: embed all queries and candidates, then FAISS nearest-neighbour (dot product) over either the 5.6M M-BEIR pool or the task-specific M-BEIR_local pool

metrics.name: Recall@5 (Recall@10 for Fashion200K and FashionIQ)
metrics.definition: follows CLIP/BLIP MSCOCO recall: a retrieved instance counts as correct if it overlaps with relevant instances

metrics.name: Error type rates (wrong modality, wrong domain, other)
metrics.definition: share of retrieval errors by category on the global pool

eval.protocol: Global-pool (M-BEIR, 5.6M) and local-pool (M-BEIR_local) retrieval; held-out experiments train on 7 datasets and test on WebQA, OVEN, CIRR; held-out figures average CLIP_SF and BLIP_FF; no seeds or significance tests.

evidence.quote: We train the model for 20 epochs using other hyperparameters as reported in the original implementations.
encompassing 1.5 million queries and a pool of 5.6 million retrieval candidates in total

results.claim: Zero-shot pretrained retrievers are near zero on the heterogeneous 5.6M pool because they retrieve the query's own modality.
results.setup: M-BEIR 5.6M pool, zero-shot CLIP/SigLIP/BLIP/BLIP2, no instruction
results.quote: all zero-shot models retrieve text instances from the global pool, leading to 0% recall rate

results.claim: Instruction-tuning raises average Recall@5 on M-BEIR (5.6M pool) over the same architecture trained multi-task without instructions: CLIP_SF 36.1 to 48.9.
results.setup: M-BEIR global pool, in-distribution (all 10 datasets seen in training); CLIP_SF multi-task vs UniIR; BLIP_FF 34.6 to 45.5 (+10.9)
results.quote: The average Recall@5 has increased by 12.8 and 10.9, respectively.
results.table: Table 3, row Avg., columns Multi. and UniIR (also Table 2 Average)

results.claim: Instruction gains are largest on cross-modality tasks 1 and 3 and negligible on within-modality tasks 2 and 5.
results.setup: M-BEIR global pool, CLIP_SF, Multi-task 15.3 vs UniIR 46.1 on task 1; task 5 gain only +1.0
results.quote: We also discovered that the largest improvement was observed in cross-modality retrieval tasks 1 and 3.

results.claim: Multi-task models without instructions retrieve the wrong modality about half the time; instruction tuning cuts it to 2.7% (CLIP_SF) and 15.2% (BLIP_FF).
results.setup: M-BEIR global pool errors; Multi-task CLIP_SF 58.8%, BLIP_FF 50.9%; UniIR CLIP_SF 2.7%, BLIP_FF 15.2%
results.quote: The Multi-task models showed a high error rate of 58.8% and 50.9% in retrieving instances with the wrong modality from the global pool.

results.claim: Best UniIR model (CLIP_SF) reaches average Recall@5 of 48.9 on the 5.6M pool versus 5.9 for zero-shot BLIP2 (the zero-shot column shown in Table 2).
results.setup: M-BEIR 5.6M pool, all datasets; zero-shot BLIP2 5.9, CLIP_SF multi-task 36.1
results.table: Table 2, row Average, columns BLIP2 and CLIPSF (Delta)
results.note: Table 2 as extracted shows only BLIP2 for the zero-shot block; Table 3 gives zero-shot CLIP average 7.9 and BLIP 5.7.

results.claim: Held-out generalisation on the 5.6M pool (Figure 5): UniIR beats multi-task (no instruction) on all held-out tasks except OVEN task 6 where both are near 9-10; averages from Table 7: multi-task CLIP_SF 20.5 / BLIP_FF 22.8 vs UniIR 27.9 / 28.7.
results.metric: held-out average Recall@5, CLIP_SF multi-task vs UniIR
results.setup: Trained on 7 datasets, tested zero-shot on WebQA, OVEN, CIRR; M-BEIR global pool; zero-shot CLIP 13.5, BLIP 11.1, SigLIP 14.1, BLIP2 11.0
results.table: Table 7, row Average, columns CLIPSF (Multi.) and CLIPSF (UniIR)
results.note: Intro says instruction tuning 'leads to +10 improvement in terms of recall@5 (Figure 5)'; Table 7 averages give about +7 (CLIP_SF +7.4, BLIP_FF +5.9) and the Figure 5 five-task means about 21.7 vs 28.3, so the +10 is not reproduced from the printed numbers (the +10.1 to +12.8 figures in Table 2/3 are in-distribution).

results.claim: Held-out generalisation on local pools (Figure 6): UniIR beats multi-task without instruction by about 4 points on average and SoTA zero-shot retrievers by more; multi-task without instruction is worse than zero-shot on some tasks.
results.setup: Trained on 7 datasets, tested on WebQA, OVEN, CIRR; M-BEIR_local; CLIP_SF multi-task 35.1 vs UniIR 40.3; BLIP_FF multi-task 32.4 vs UniIR 35.2; zero-shot SigLIP 35.5
results.table: Table 8, row Average, columns CLIPSF (Multi.) and CLIPSF (UniIR)

results.claim: On M-BEIR_local, multi-task training with instructions helps BLIP_FF strongly (single-task 37.1 to 46.8) but CLIP_SF only slightly (49.4 to 50.6), and multi-task without instructions leaves CLIP_SF at 49.4.
results.setup: M-BEIR_local, all 10 datasets seen in training; ST=single-task fine-tuning; BLIP_FF multi-task without instruction 45.8; gain +9.7 vs single-task
results.quote: UniIR (BLIPFF) greatly outperforms its single-task counterpart by an average of 9.7% on R@5
results.note: Intro credits the +9.7 to 'multi-task training in UniIR(BLIP)'; Table 6 delta is UniIR (with instructions) minus single-task, and multi-task without instructions is 45.8 (+8.7 over ST), so most of this gain is from multi-task training, not instructions, for BLIP_FF.

results.claim: UniIR surpasses the best zero-shot retriever (SigLIP) on M-BEIR_local.
results.metric: average Recall@5 on M-BEIR_local, UniIR CLIP_SF
results.setup: M-BEIR_local; SigLIP 37.2 is best zero-shot; UniIR BLIP_FF 46.8
results.quote: our UniIR models (CLIPSF) and (BLIPFF) surpass it by a significant margin, with average R@5 values of 50.6% and 46.8% respectively

results.claim: Aligning fusion with pretraining architecture helps: CLIP with score fusion beats CLIP with randomly initialised feature-fusion layers by 5.7 average Recall@5 and BLIP feature fusion beats BLIP score fusion by 2.8.
results.setup: M-BEIR global pool; UniIR CLIP_SF 48.9 vs CLIP_FF 43.3; BLIP_FF 45.5 vs BLIP_SF 42.7
results.quote: with an average improvement of 5.7 and 2.8 for CLIP and BLIP, respectively
results.note: The text then says task 8 dropped 'from 52.4 to 46.3, for the latter' but 46.3 is the CLIP_FF value in Table 5 and 52.4 is CLIP_SF, so 'the latter' is misworded.

results.claim: Zero-shot SigLIP is the strongest zero-shot baseline on M-BEIR_local on average, CLIP on news.
results.setup: M-BEIR_local zero-shot: SigLIP 37.2, CLIP 32.5, BLIP 26.8, BLIP2 24.8

limits: Authors concede 'the existing model performance is still relatively far from perfect indicating ample room for future improvement' and defer stronger vision-language backbones and large-scale pretraining to future work.
Only CLIP and BLIP ViT-L backbones are fine-tuned; optimizer, learning rate, schedule, seeds and variance are not given, and there are no significance tests.

Generalisation to unseen data is shown on only three held-out datasets (WebQA, OVEN, CIRR), which share task types with held-in data and, for tasks 2, 3, 6, 8, share domains; the held-out figures average CLIP_SF and BLIP_FF; the held-in/held-out numbers per backbone differ sharply.

The ablation attributing gains to instructions compares against multi-task training without instructions; the instruction-versus-no-instruction effect is measured both in-distribution (Table 2/3) and held-out (Fig 5/6, Tables 7/8); the held-out gain from instructions is smaller (about 4 to 7 points) than the paper's stated +10.
Internal inconsistencies: intro says 300K training instances while Table 1 totals 1.1M; intro cites Figure 6 for held-out generalisation of the best model but Figure 6 is the local-pool experiment.
Instructions are written by the authors (4 per task-dataset pair, 64 in total); robustness to unseen instruction phrasing is not tested.
Candidate pools were trimmed to balance data (e.g. VisualNews, OVEN, InfoSeek), so the 5.6M pool is not the full original corpora.
Venue: only an arXiv v1 stamp (cs.CV, 28 Nov 2023) is printed; no conference name appears in the PDF.

separate vision and text encoders whose per-modality vectors are combined by a weighted sum, so the similarity is a weighted sum of within- and cross-modality scores
integrates features during the encoding phase with mixed-modality attention layers into one vector for multimodal queries or candidates

figures.caption: We build a universal multimodal information retriever UniIR through instruction tuning. UniIR is capable of accepting any form of query and instruction to retrieve information in any modality.
figures.why: Shows instruction + heterogeneous query/candidate mix at a glance

figures.caption: (a) Score-level fusion encodes each modality into a single feature; (b) CLIP feature-level fusion (CLIP_FF) fuses two modalities into a single feature with a mix-modality transformer layer; (c) BLIP feature-level fusion (BLIP_FF) adopts cross-attention to output a single feature vector.
figures.why: Architecture comparison of the fusion variants

figures.caption: The overview of M-BEIR training/validation/test set.
figures.why: Datasets, tasks, split sizes and pool sizes in one table

figures.caption: Visualization of top 5 retrieved candidates from M-BEIR with 3 models on EDIS. Without instructions, zero-shot and multi-task training models mostly retrieve the wrong modality (text-only).
figures.why: Shows the wrong-modality failure the instruction fixes

figures.caption: Held-out dataset generalization experiments on M-BEIR (and M-BEIR_local): train a Multi-task and a UniIR model on 7 held-in datasets and test on 3 held-out datasets (WebQA, OVEN, CIRR).
figures.why: The held-out evidence for the generalisation claim

code.snippet: c* = argmax_{c in C} [ f(q, q_inst)^T . f(c) ]
f(q_i, q_t, q_inst) = w1 f_I(q_i) + w2 f_T(q_t, q_inst);  f(c_i, c_t) = w3 f_I(c_i) + w4 f_T(c_t)
